content: The management of second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) involves addressing co-infections and comorbidities, ensuring adherence to ART, and retaining patients in care. Innovative service delivery models, such as integration, decentralization, and task-shifting, are essential. Additionally, the availability of human resources, laboratory and diagnostic services, and effective procurement and supply management systems are critical components. Decision-making regarding what actions to take, where, and when should be guided by a structured process, supported by relevant data and key parameters. Implementation considerations and tools for cost analysis and planning are also necessary. Programmatic and clinical monitoring and evaluation should focus on the implications of new recommendations, tracking the outcomes of scaling up ART access, and monitoring HIV drug resistance and ART toxicity. The implementation of these guidelines contributes to global health goals, including universal access to HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support. These align with the objectives outlined in the 2006 and 2011 Political Declarations on HIV/AIDS, as well as the Global Health Sector Strategy on HIV/AIDS (2011–2015) and the Global Plan to eliminate new HIV infections among children by 2015 while keeping their mothers alive. Specific targets for 2015 included reducing HIV infections among young people by 50%, reducing new HIV infections in children by 90%, decreasing HIV-related deaths by 25%, halving HIV-related maternal deaths, and reducing tuberculosis-related deaths by 50%. Additionally, the goal was to have 15 million people on ART in lowand middle-income countries. In the long term, these guidelines aim to support universal health coverage, a cornerstone of the post-2015 development agenda. The guidelines are based on a public health approach, as recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) since 2002. This approach emphasizes broad access to high-quality services at the population level, using simplified and standardized methods. It seeks to balance the implementation of the best-proven standards of care with what is feasible on a large scale in resource-limited settings. Strengthening health systems through innovation and learning is a key focus. Recommendations and innovations in service delivery should enhance the continuum of HIV care and broader health systems, particularly primary and chronic care. HIV services are increasingly integrated into lower-level health facilities in high-burden settings, with prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) services becoming core components of maternal and child health services. Integration of HIV, tuberculosis (TB), hepatitis, drug dependence, and harm reduction services is also advancing. As individuals on ART age and HIV becomes a chronic, manageable condition, integrating HIV services with non-communicable disease care will become increasingly important. These guidelines promote adapting service delivery models to strengthen the continuum of HIV care, ensuring timely ART initiation, appropriate referrals, and lifelong adherence to treatment. In the context of limited financial resources and competing priorities, countries must make strategic choices to optimize the effectiveness and efficiency of HIV programs. This includes prioritizing ART for those most in need, exploring earlier treatment initiation for certain populations, and improving adherence and retention through innovative service delivery. Efforts should also focus on integrating ART into diverse settings, strengthening links between services, and optimizing drug regimens and diagnostics to enhance affordability and accessibility. Promoting human rights and health equity is fundamental. Access to HIV prevention, treatment, care, and support should be recognized as a universal right. Informed consent, particularly for HIV testing and ART initiation, must always be obtained, and confidentiality safeguards must be in place. Implementation of these guidelines should be informed by local contexts, including HIV epidemiology, resource availability, health system capacity, and cost-effectiveness. Strong recommendations for specific service delivery approaches should not override effective models already in place within a country. The 2013 consolidated guidelines compile new and existing recommendations across the continuum of HIV care, including diagnosis, general care, and the strategic use of ART for treatment and prevention. These recommendations were developed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) system, ensuring a robust evidence-based approach. Community consultations and systematic reviews informed the development process, with input from diverse stakeholders, including civil society and networks of people living with HIV. The guidelines emphasize the importance of monitoring and evaluation, dissemination, and adaptation to local contexts. They aim to support countries in scaling up ART access, improving service delivery, and achieving global health goals.
